title: One action at a time
hook: build your life action by action; no one can stop you doing each well (Meditations 8.32)
tomorrow: Not the whole life at once

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was matter: the thing, the act, the meaning, and being good today, not tomorrow. Your line was what it means.

A stone wall on an old farm. No mortar, no blueprint. Somebody built it by picking up one stone, turning it until it fit, setting it down, and picking up the next. When a stone was too big, they didn't quit; they set it aside and found one that fit the gap. Generations later, the wall still stands. Marcus Aurelius thought a life gets built the same way, and this part of the path takes its title from today's entry.
screen: `A DRY STONE WALL.` → `ONE STONE, THEN THE NEXT.` → `A LIFE BUILT THE SAME WAY.`

segments.voice: In Meditations eight, thirty-two, Marcus says you have to put your life together action by action, and if each action does its job as far as it can, be satisfied. Not each life. Each action. That's the unit. Then something bold: no one can stop you from making each action do its job. Someone might object that some outside thing will get in the way. Marcus answers: nothing can stop you acting justly, with self-control and with good sense. The world can block your plans; it can't block the way you meet the block. Then the most practical part. Maybe something stops the particular action you intended. Fine. Accept the obstacle gracefully, turn to what is possible, and a new action takes its place, one that fits the same building. That's the farmer setting aside the stone that's too big. The wall keeps rising. And this frees you. If your life is one giant project, every setback threatens the whole thing. Built action by action, a setback is just one stone that didn't fit, and the next stone is always there. You don't need to fix your whole life today, only do the next action well. Marcus wrote it for an emperor's days. It fits a stack of laundry just as well.
screen: `BUILD YOUR LIFE ACTION BY ACTION.` · `NO ONE CAN STOP YOU ACTING WELL.` · `BLOCKED? A NEW ACTION FITS.` · `THE NEXT STONE IS ALWAYS THERE.` · then, large: `ONE ACTION AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Don't think about your whole life, or even your whole day. Ask only: what is the very next action I'll take after this sit, standing up, making a call, washing a cup, and how would I do it well? If your mind jumps ahead to the rest of the list, set the list down and come back to the next stone.
Marcus, who said a life is put together action by action, and when one is blocked, another that fits takes its place. Today's word.
Your line: pick up the next stone. The wall rises one fit at a time. That's day six hundred one.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often treat their day as a series of single actions to do well, and when a plan is blocked, they accept it and choose the next possible action rather than abandoning the whole.

notes: Meditations 8.32 paraphrased: build up life action by action, content if each fulfills its duty as far as possible; no one can hinder this; something external may stand in the way, but nothing hinders acting justly, soberly and wisely; if some action is hindered, accept it and pass to what is allowed, and another action takes its place that fits the composition. Confirm.
The 'reserve clause' (hupexhairesis) framing in the trapdoor is interpretive; confirm that 8.32 is fairly read this way.
'Practice' from praxis: confirm etymology (via Greek praktikos and Latin practica).
The part title ('one action at a time') is this path's label, drawn from 8.32.
Reviewer softened the claim that Marcus wrote this while running an empire at war: where and when book 8 was written is unknown; the line now refers only to the wars and plague of his reign. Confirm.
